analysis.one_liner: Repeals the ACA individual mandate penalty so no one is fined for going uninsured.
analysis.headline: The House passed the repeal on Dec. 19, 2019 on an 86–62 party-line vote (86 Republicans for, all 62 House Democrats against), but the Senate adjourned without taking it up.
analysis.plain_summary: Health insurance sellers can refuse to sell you a plan, charge you more, or bury real limits in the fine print. For 45 years, when that happened, state insurance regulators could order the seller to pay what it owed you — but few people knew, and few bothered to claim. H.R. 4341 said every insurer must print a simple notice on the claim form itself telling you what was denied or underpaid, that you can appeal, that you may be owed money the company could be ordered to pay, and how to ask a state insurance regulator to act. It also let state insurance regulators act without a prior complaint and send unresolved disputes to court. Because most individual and group plans are sold by companies incorporated outside your state, it required those out-of-state insurers to follow your state regulator's order as if it were an order from their own home state. The House passed it 86–62 with every Republican in favor and every Democrat against, but the Senate never took it up and the 2024 session ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The tens of millions of Americans with private health insurance. When an insurer denies or short-pays a claim, readers learn from the denial letter itself that they can appeal, ask a state insurance regulator for help, or take the dispute to court. Today many never learn any of this. Since unpaid claims usually go unclaimed, insurers keep that money. HR 4341 would reduce what companies can quietly keep by making sure every policyholder sees the notice. It would also let state regulators order insurers to pay before anyone files a complaint, and make companies incorporated elsewhere obey an order from your state.

how_it_helps.text: Requires insurers to include a specific, plain statement on the claim form telling you: what was denied or not paid in full, that you have the right to appeal, that a state insurance regulator may order the company to pay you, and that you can ask the regulator for help.
Requires insurers to list in the policy documents, every time the policy renews, the name and contact of the state insurance regulator with authority over claims in your state.
Lets a state insurance regulator order payment on its own initiative, before any policyholder files a complaint — many people never file one because they do not know they can win.

Makes insurers incorporated in another state obey an order from your state's insurance regulator the same way they obey orders from their own state — closing the loophole that lets companies incorporate in one state but sell to every other.
Lets your state send a dispute between an insurer and a policyholder to court.

analysis.who_pays: Insurers that pay less than they owe would lose some of that windfall and would have to change claim forms and customer notices. Insurers that already pay what they owe would notice no difference.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers that pay less than they owe

drawbacks.text: Insurers say increased cost of compliance could add to premiums, which are already high. The bill sets no cap or audit to prevent that argument from being overstated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill takes a 45-year-old state power — ordering insurers to pay what they owe — and makes it visible and usable to the people it protects: it changes the form they actually read, tells them the regulator's name every renewal, lets the regulator act before anyone files, and makes out-of-state insurers obey. The compliance cost to insurers is minor and in line with existing state disclosure rules. This is a real, if modest, shift of power toward policyholders.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 86–62 on Dec. 19, 2019, but the Senate adjourned for the session without ever taking it up.

narrative.text: Introduced Aug. 2, 2019, and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
Brought to the floor under a rule; the House Rules Committee reported the rule on Dec. 18, 2019.
Passed 86–62 on Dec. 19, 2019: 86 Republicans for, 62 Democrats against, no Republican against, no Democrat for.
Received in the Senate, read twice, referred to the Senate Finance Committee — no further action before the end of the session on Jan. 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers that deny or underpay claims keep what policyholders never learn they can recover. State regulators who wanted the power to order payment on their own initiative did not get it.

industries.note: Today, unpaid claims that policyholders never learn they can recover are effectively a windfall to insurers. HR 4341 would take away a chunk of that by putting the appeal-and-regulator notice directly on the claim form and letting regulators order payment without a complaint.
Would gain the power to order payment on their own initiative, without a prior complaint, and to make out-of-state insurers obey their orders.
Would be subject to the same notice and regulator-order requirements, with the same out-of-state compliance rule.
